title: lightweight kernel observability: token-path kernel mapping and sampled nvtx envelopes
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Objective: Add a low-overhead, request-correlated kernel observability layer that maps per-kernel execution to token-level execution paths (prefill vs decode) so we can attribute latency/cost regressions to specific attention kernels and scheduling decisions. This ticket covers the end-to-end plan: a compact NVTX naming envelope, request-scoped kernel tags, an adaptive sampling mode for heavy requests, exporter mappings to our trace system, and dashboards/alerting to detect kernel-caused regressions.

Background and rationale: We currently have coarse kernel metrics and sampled NVTX spans that are useful for aggregate analysis but hard to tie back to the token execution path for a specific request. This makes diagnosing regressions from kernel selection (e.g., f32 vs int8 kernels, attention vs fused attention) and prefill/decode schedule interactions time-consuming. We need instrumentation that: 
- correlates kernel-level timing with request IDs and token indices,
- keeps overhead negligible for tail latency and throughput (target <2% p99 latency overhead), and
- provides a sampled dense telemetry mode for deeper investigation without continuous cost.

Scope and deliverables:
1) Naming envelope: Define a compact NVTX name format that encodes: request short-id, phase (prefill|decode), token-range (if applicable), kernel-category (attention|dense|kv-cache|decoder-op), and optional kernel-variant tag (e.g., int8-qkv, fused-attn-v2). Document the encoding and backward-compatible parsing rules.
2) Kernel tag API: Implement a runtime API to attach a 64-bit kernel tag to GPU work submissions and NVTX ranges. The tag format maps to the NVTX name and is friendly to downstream span-aggregation.
3) Request-scoped stitching: Emit a lightweight span at request start with a request-id and deterministic short-hash that is included in kernel NVTX envelopes so traces can stitch request -> kernels -> metrics in the trace backend without heavy stack traces.
4) Adaptive sampler: Add a sampler that promotes dense NVTX capture and full kernel counters for a configurable fraction of requests based on heuristics (latency outliers, model type, customer tier). Sampler decisions must be visible in traces and metrics.
5) Exporter and dashboard: Map kernel tags to user-friendly labels in our trace exporter, create a per-request kernel timing dashboard (top N kernels by cumulative time and count), and add a regression alert if any single kernel increases median time by >30% over baseline for a model-route.
6) Tests and perf safety: Microbenchmarks to verify <2% overhead for standard traffic, and an integration test that validates request->kernel mapping for both prefill and decode flows.

Success criteria:
- Engineers can reliably find the kernel responsible for a p99 latency increase in <30 minutes for a real customer workload.
- Sampling mode can be safely enabled in staging with <5% additional GPU load.
- Dashboards surface kernel-level regressions for top 5 models by traffic within 2 minutes of occurrence.

Out-of-scope for this ticket: full-run nvprof-style traces, kernel-level memory profiling, external HSM/KMS integrations. Those will be follow-ups if we need deeper insights.

implementation_notes: Implementation uses a compact request short-hash to keep NVTX string length small (<=64 chars). Kernel tags are encoded as a base36 token to save bytes in NVTX names emitted by the runtime. The sampler uses a two-tier heuristic: (1) deterministic downsample by model-route percentage, and (2) dynamic promotion for latency outliers computed by the routing proxy. Tracing backend mapping will translate base36 kernel tokens to labels via a small lookup table pushed with each deploy.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: NVTX name bloat could increase CUDA driver overhead. Mitigation: keep envelope <=64 characters, and fall back to numeric tag-only NVTX name when length limit approached. Risk: sampler could spike GPU/IO if misconfigured. Mitigation: enforce rate-limits and per-GPU quotas in sampler and require a safety knob to cap dense-capture rate.
next_steps: 1) Merge PR and smoke canary deployment to dedicated-staging pool. 2) Run 48h perf soak with production-like traffic and evaluate overhead and trace utility. 3) Iterate labeling mapping and add regression alert rules. 4) Create runbook for on-call to use kernel-map dashboard for triage.
